This item fixes finite combinatorial vocabulary for outcome laws of a
two-station comparison. No physical interpretation, measurement model,
dynamics or locality assertion is made here; the physical readings are fixed
on the page of this pair. No choice principle is used.

**(a) Binary correlation model.** Let $I$ and $J$ be finite nonempty sets, the
**setting labels** of the two stations, and put
$\Sigma:=\{-1,+1\}$ for the common **outcome labels**. A **binary correlation
model** on $(I,J)$ is a family
$$\mu=(\mu_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J},\qquad \mu_{ij}:\Sigma\times\Sigma\to[0,1],$$
of functions with the normalization
$$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=1 \qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\in I\times J$$
([[def-finite-sum]]). Each $\mu_{ij}$ is the **joint law** of the setting pair
$(i,j)$: it is the outcome-weight function of a finite probability space on
the four outcomes $\Sigma\times\Sigma$ in the sense of
[[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], and sums over $\Sigma\times\Sigma$
are finite sums.

**(b) Marginals.** For $(i,j)\in I\times J$ the **marginal law of the first
station** and the **marginal law of the second station** are
$$\mu^{A}_{ij}(\varepsilon):=\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta), \qquad \mu^{B}_{ij}(\delta):=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta), \qquad \varepsilon,\delta\in\Sigma .$$

**(c) No-signalling.** The model $\mu$ is **no-signalling** when the marginal
law of the first station does not depend on the distant setting,
$\mu^{A}_{ij}=\mu^{A}_{ij'}$ for all $i\in I$ and all $j,j'\in J$, and the
marginal law of the second station does not depend on the distant setting,
$\mu^{B}_{ij}=\mu^{B}_{i'j}$ for all $j\in J$ and all $i,i'\in I$. The word is
used as a name for this pair of identities about the tables; no spatial or
causal claim is attached to it.

**(d) Correlations and the CHSH functional.** Assume $I=J=\{0,1\}$. The
**correlation** of the setting pair $(i,j)$ and the **CHSH functional** of the
model are the real numbers
$$E_{ij}(\mu):=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma} \varepsilon\,\delta\,\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta), \qquad S(\mu):=E_{00}(\mu)+E_{01}(\mu)+E_{10}(\mu)-E_{11}(\mu).$$

**(e) Status.** Clauses (a)-(d) introduce finite tables, their marginals, the
no-signalling identities and one linear functional of four correlations. They
assert no physical assumption, no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law
for a real apparatus and no statement about nature; the identification of a
laboratory arrangement with a model $\mu$ is a separate physical matter.

Let $\mu$ be a binary correlation model on the finite setting sets $I,J$ with
outcome labels $\Sigma=\{-1,+1\}$
([[def-nrqm-bell-binary-correlation-models]]). No choice principle is used in
this definition.

**(a) Local-response representation.** A **local-response representation** of
$\mu$ is a tuple consisting of a probability space $(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda},
\mathbb P)$ ([[def-measure-space]], [[def-probability-measure]]) and two
families of **response laws**
$$(\alpha_{i})_{i\in I},\qquad (\beta_{j})_{j\in J},$$
where for each $i\in I$ the function
$\alpha_{i}:\Lambda\times\Sigma\to[0,1]$ has the two properties
$$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\alpha_{i}(\lambda,\varepsilon)=1\quad(\lambda\in\Lambda), \qquad \lambda\mapsto\alpha_{i}(\lambda,+1)\ \text{is measurable}$$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), and the family
$(\beta_{j})_{j\in J}$ has the same two properties; and the **representation
identity**
$$\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta) =\int_{\Lambda}\alpha_{i}(\lambda,\varepsilon)\,\beta_{j}(\lambda,\delta)\, d\mathbb P(\lambda) =\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\!\left[\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\, \beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)\right]$$
holds for every $(i,j)\in I\times J$ and every
$(\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma$. The integrand is a product of two
bounded measurable $[0,1]$-valued functions, so the expectation exists as a
finite number ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]). The functions
$\alpha_{i}(\cdot,-1)=1-\alpha_{i}(\cdot,+1)$ and likewise for $\beta_{j}$ are
measurable as well. The variable $\lambda$ is called the **specification**
of the representation; it is a mathematical index, and no physical
interpretation is asserted.

**(b) Response functions (deterministic form).** Equip the finite outcome set
$\Sigma=\{-1,+1\}$ with its discrete $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal P(\Sigma)$.
A local-response representation **has response functions** when there are
measurable maps
$a_{i}:(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda})\to(\Sigma,\mathcal P(\Sigma))$ $(i\in I)$
and $b_{j}:(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda})\to(\Sigma,\mathcal P(\Sigma))$
$(j\in J)$ with
$$\alpha_{i}(\lambda,\varepsilon)=\mathbf 1_{\{a_{i}=\varepsilon\}}(\lambda), \qquad \beta_{j}(\lambda,\delta)=\mathbf 1_{\{b_{j}=\delta\}}(\lambda),$$
in which case the representation identity reads
$$\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta) =\mathbb P\bigl(\{a_{i}=\varepsilon\}\cap\{b_{j}=\delta\}\bigr).$$
The deterministic form is a special case of clause (a): it is obtained by
setting the response laws to the Dirac laws at $a_{i}(\lambda)$ and
$b_{j}(\lambda)$. In this form one and the same specification space and the
same single-station functions $a_{i}$ and $b_{j}$ serve every setting
pair, and the response of a station depends on the specification and on that
station's own setting only.

**(c) Terminology.** The two mathematical features named by **local response**
are: (i) a single specification space carrying the probability law used for
every setting pair (setting-independence), and (ii) per-station response laws
that do not depend on the distant station's setting. A model that admits such
a representation is also called a **local model** of the tables in the
literature; the representation is an existence statement about the tables and
asserts no determinism, no mechanism, no dynamics and no causal relation. In
particular clause (a) permits probabilistic responses and does not require
the response functions of clause (b).

**(d) Status.** Clauses (a)-(c) fix vocabulary. They assert no physical
assumption and no property of any laboratory arrangement; whether a declared
physical model of a comparison admits a representation of this form is a
mathematical question about its tables, and the physical reading of that
question is fixed on the page of this pair.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

derivations.claim: [Marginal of the first station] Fix $i\in I$, $j\in J$ and $\varepsilon\in\Sigma$. By [F1] and the definition of the marginal, $\mu^{A}_{ij}(\varepsilon)=\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\bigl[\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)\bigr]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\bigl[\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)\bigr]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)]$, where the second equality is the representation identity, the third is the finite linearity of [F3], and the last is the normalization of [F2]. The resulting expression involves $i$ and $\varepsilon$ only, so $\mu^{A}_{ij}(\varepsilon)=\mu^{A}_{ij'}(\varepsilon)$ for every $j'\in J$; as $(\varepsilon,i,j)$ were arbitrary this is the first-station half of (a).

[Marginal of the second station] The same computation with the roles of the two stations exchanged, summing this time over $\varepsilon\in\Sigma$ and using the normalization $\sum_{\varepsilon}\alpha_{i}(\lambda,\varepsilon)=1$ of [F2], gives $\mu^{B}_{ij}(\delta)=\sum_{\varepsilon}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)]$ for every $\delta\in\Sigma$, an expression free of $i$; hence $\mu^{B}_{ij}=\mu^{B}_{i'j}$ for all $i,i'\in I$, the second-station half of (a).

[Assembly and contrapositive] Steps 1.1 and 1.2 give the two setting-independence identities, which by [F1] is exactly no-signalling of $\mu$; this is (a). For (b), if a model admits a local-response representation then (a) makes it no-signalling, so a model that is not no-signalling admits none.

boundaries.reason: I and J are finite nonempty setting sets by clause (a) of the definition of a binary correlation model; no empty setting family occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 1.2 use only the normalization of the response laws, so response laws assigning probability 0 to +1 are covered.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 make no use of the cardinality of I or J, so the case |I|=|J|=1 is included.
A point-mass table has a representation with Dirac response laws and satisfies the conclusion; steps 1.1 and 1.2 do not assume nondegeneracy.

boundaries.reason: The proposition involves no interval endpoints or boundary parameters.

boundaries.evidence: No choice principle is used; the statement quantifies over given data and the proof uses only them (steps 1.1 and 2.1).

boundaries.reason: Clause (b) is the contrapositive of clause (a), not a biconditional; the single direction is covered by steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1.
The proposition contains no reverse implication; representability implies no-signalling only.

risk_review.notes: Checked all three steps and exact Definition clauses (a)-(c). Both response normalizations appear in corrected F2 and contract quotation. All functions are bounded measurable, so finite expectation linearity applies. Each marginal equals expectation of its own station law; contrapositive is correct and converse is not claimed. Finite nonempty setting sets, both outcome labels and deterministic endpoints checked. No choice or empirical premise; reader normalization repair accepted, no refuter finding.

derivations.claim: [Correlations through local means] Fix $(i,j)\in\{0,1\}^{2}$. By [F1] and [F3], $E_{ij}(\mu)=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\varepsilon\delta\,\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\bigl[\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\varepsilon\delta\,\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)\bigr]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\bigl[\bigl(\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\varepsilon\,\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\delta\,\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)\bigr)\bigr]=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[a_{i}b_{j}]$ with the local means of [F2], the inner factorizations being the distributive law in $\mathbb R$ for the two-term sums over $\Sigma$.

[Pointwise bound] Let $u,v,s,t\in[-1,1]$. Then $|s(u+v)+t(u-v)|\le|u+v|+|u-v|$ by the triangle inequality and $|s|,|t|\le1$. For real $u,v$ one has $|u+v|+|u-v|=2\max(|u|,|v|)$: if $|v|\le|u|$ then both $u+v$ and $u-v$ have the sign of $u$ (for $|v|\le|u|$ neither crosses $0$), so the sum is $|2u|=2\max(|u|,|v|)$, and the case $|v|>|u|$ is symmetric with the roles of $u$ and $v$ exchanged. $$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

$f : X \to [0,+\infty]$ be measurable. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ define

$$s_k := \sum_{j=0}^{k2^k-1} j2^{-k}\, \mathbf{1}_{\{j2^{-k} \le f < (j+1)2^{-k}\}} + k\,\mathbf{1}_{\{f \ge k\}}.$$

Then each $s_k$ is a simple measurable function,

$$0 \le s_k \le s_{k+1} \le f,$$

and $s_k(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in X$. If $E \subseteq X$ is a set on which
$f \le M < +\infty$, then $s_k \to f$ uniformly on $E$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $\mu$ be a binary correlation model on the setting sets $I=J=\{0,1\}$
with outcome labels $\Sigma=\{-1,+1\}$, with correlations $E_{ij}(\mu)$ and
CHSH functional $S(\mu)$ as in
[[def-nrqm-bell-binary-correlation-models]] clauses (d), and suppose that
$\mu$ admits a local-response representation with response laws
$(\alpha_{i})_{i\in I}$, $(\beta_{j})_{j\in J}$ on a probability space
$(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda},\mathbb P)$
([[def-nrqm-bell-local-response-representation]]). Then
$$\bigl|S(\mu)\bigr|\le 2 .$$

asserts no measurement, no dynamics, no spatial or causal structure, and it
contains no physics. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: [$\mathbb P_{D}$ is a probability measure] Since $\mathbb P(D)>0$, the definition of $\mathbb P_{D}$ is meaningful; it is nonnegative and $\mathbb P_{D}(\Lambda)=\mathbb P(\Lambda\cap D)/\mathbb P(D)=1$. For pairwise disjoint $A_{n}\in\Sigma_{\Lambda}$ with union $A$, the sets $A_{n}\cap D$ are pairwise disjoint with union $A\cap D$, so countable additivity of $\mathbb P$ [F2] gives $\mathbb P_{D}(A)=\mathbb P(A\cap D)/\mathbb P(D)=\sum_{n}\mathbb P(A_{n}\cap D)/\mathbb P(D)=\sum_{n}\mathbb P_{D}(A_{n})$; hence $\mathbb P_{D}$ is a probability measure on $(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda})$.

[Indicators] Let $A\in\Sigma_{\Lambda}$. Then $\mathbf 1_{D}\mathbf 1_{A}=\mathbf 1_{A\cap D}$, and [F3] applied to the probability space $(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda},\mathbb P)$ gives $\int\mathbf 1_{D}\mathbf 1_{A}\,d\mathbb P=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{A\cap D}]=\mathbb P(A\cap D)$, while [F3] applied to $(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda},\mathbb P_{D})$ gives $\int\mathbf 1_{A}\,d\mathbb P_{D}=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_{D}}[\mathbf 1_{A}]=\mathbb P_{D}(A)=\mathbb P(A\cap D)/\mathbb P(D)$; hence $\int_{\Lambda}\mathbf 1_{A}\,d\mathbb P_{D}=\mathbb P(D)^{-1}\int_{\Lambda}\mathbf 1_{D}\mathbf 1_{A}\,d\mathbb P$.

[Nonnegative simple functions] By [F4] and the definition of the integral of a nonnegative simple function, both sides of the identity of step 2.1 are linear in the integrand over finite nonnegative combinations; hence for every nonnegative simple function $s$ on $(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda})$ one has $\int_{\Lambda}s\,d\mathbb P_{D}=\mathbb P(D)^{-1}\int_{\Lambda}\mathbf 1_{D}s\,d\mathbb P$.

[Normalization] By [F1] and [F4], $\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}\mu^{D}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\mathbb P(D)^{-1}\int\mathbf 1_{D}\bigl(\sum_{\varepsilon}\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{\delta}\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)\bigr)d\mathbb P=\mathbb P(D)^{-1}\int\mathbf 1_{D}\,d\mathbb P=\mathbb P(D)/\mathbb P(D)=1$, the last equality by the indicator identity of step 2.1 with $A=\Lambda$, and each $\mu^{D}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)\ge0$ by nonnegativity of the integrand; hence $\mu^{D}$ is a binary correlation model on $(I,J)$. Together with step 1.1 this is (a).

[Bounded measurable functions] Let $f\ge0$ be measurable and bounded, say $0\le f\le M<+\infty$. By [F5] choose an increasing sequence $(s_{k})$ of nonnegative simple functions with $s_{k}\uparrow f$; then $\mathbf 1_{D}s_{k}\uparrow\mathbf 1_{D}f$, and monotone convergence [F5] applied to the measures $\mathbb P_{D}$ and $\mathbb P$ gives $\int s_{k}\,d\mathbb P_{D}\uparrow\int f\,d\mathbb P_{D}$ and $\int\mathbf 1_{D}s_{k}\,d\mathbb P\uparrow\int\mathbf 1_{D}f\,d\mathbb P$. Passing to the limit in the identity of step 3.1, valid for every $k$, yields $\int_{\Lambda}f\,d\mathbb P_{D}=\mathbb P(D)^{-1}\int_{\Lambda}\mathbf 1_{D}f\,d\mathbb P$.

[Representation over $\mathbb P_{D}$] Fix $i,j,\varepsilon,\delta$ and put $f:=\alpha_{i}(\cdot,\varepsilon)\beta_{j}(\cdot,\delta)$. By [F1] $f$ is a product of two measurable $[0,1]$-valued functions, hence measurable and bounded with $0\le f\le1$. Step 4.1 gives $\int f\,d\mathbb P_{D}=\mathbb P(D)^{-1}\int\mathbf 1_{D}f\,d\mathbb P=\mu^{D}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)$ by the definition of the $D$-conditional tables; this is (b).

[Bound and assembly] Step 5.1 exhibits a local-response representation of $\mu^{D}$ with the same response laws over the probability space $(\Lambda,\Sigma_{\Lambda},\mathbb P_{D})$; hence [F6] applies to $\mu^{D}$ and gives $|S(\mu^{D})|\le2$ when $I=J=\{0,1\}$, which is (c). Steps 1.1 and 3.2 prove (a) and step 5.1 proves (b).

The zero function is bounded and step 4.1 applies, both sides vanishing; step 1.1 covers P_D of the empty set.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: [Projections] Fix a unit $a$ and $\varepsilon\in\Sigma$. By [F2], $P_{a,\varepsilon}^{*}=\tfrac12(I+\varepsilon\sigma_{a}^{*})=\tfrac12(I+\varepsilon\sigma_{a})=P_{a,\varepsilon}$ and $P_{a,\varepsilon}^{2}=\tfrac14(I+2\varepsilon\sigma_{a}+\varepsilon^{2}\sigma_{a}^{2})=\tfrac14(2I+2\varepsilon\sigma_{a})=\tfrac12(I+\varepsilon\sigma_{a})=P_{a,\varepsilon}$ using $\varepsilon^{2}=1$ and $\sigma_{a}^{2}=I$; hence $P_{a,\varepsilon}$ is an orthogonal projection. Moreover $P_{a,+}+P_{a,-}=I$ and $P_{a,+}P_{a,-}=\tfrac14(I-\sigma_{a}^{2})=0$, which is (a).

[Orthonormal basis] By [F3], $\|\Psi\|^{2}=\tfrac12(\|e_{+}\otimes e_{-}\|^{2}+\|e_{-}\otimes e_{+}\|^{2})=1$ and $\|q\|^{2}=1$, and the inner products pair the four displayed vectors as $0$ or $1$: for instance $\langle\Psi,q\rangle=\tfrac12(1-1)=0$ and $\langle\Psi,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+})\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\langle e_{+},e_{+}\rangle\langle e_{-},e_{+}\rangle-\langle e_{-},e_{+}\rangle\langle e_{+},e_{+}\rangle\bigr)=0$ by the product formula of [F3]. Since the four elementary tensors already form an orthonormal basis of the four-dimensional space $V\widehat\otimes V$, so do the four mutually orthogonal unit vectors $\Psi,q,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+}),\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})$; this is (b).

[Local Pauli operators on $\Psi$] Using [F1] and [F4] term by term, $(\sigma_{z}\otimes I)\Psi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})+\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\bigr)=q$ and $(I\otimes\sigma_{z})\Psi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(-\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})-\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\bigr)=-q$; further $(\sigma_{x}\otimes I)\Psi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})-\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+})\bigr)$, $(I\otimes\sigma_{x})\Psi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+})-\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})\bigr)$, $(\sigma_{y}\otimes I)\Psi=\tfrac{i}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+})+\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})\bigr)$ and $(I\otimes\sigma_{y})\Psi=\tfrac{-i}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+})+\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})\bigr)$, all of which are linear combinations of the three basis vectors $q,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+}),\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})$ orthogonal to $\Psi$ by step 1.2; hence $\langle(\sigma_{i}\otimes I)\Psi,\Psi\rangle=0=\langle(I\otimes\sigma_{i})\Psi,\Psi\rangle$ for $i=x,y,z$, and by the linearity of [F4] in the first tensor argument, $\langle(\sigma_{a}\otimes I)\Psi,\Psi\rangle=0=\langle(I\otimes\sigma_{b})\Psi,\Psi\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

[Product Pauli operators on $\Psi$] Term-by-term application of [F1] and [F4] gives $(\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x)\Psi=(\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y)\Psi=(\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z)\Psi=-\Psi$. Put $r_+:=(\kappa(e_+\otimes e_+)+\kappa(e_-\otimes e_-))/\sqrt2$ and $r_-:=(\kappa(e_+\otimes e_+)-\kappa(e_-\otimes e_-))/\sqrt2$. The six mixed products are $(\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_y)\Psi=-iq$, $(\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_x)\Psi=iq$, $(\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_z)\Psi=-r_+$, $(\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_x)\Psi=r_+$, $(\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_z)\Psi=ir_-$ and $(\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_y)\Psi=-ir_-$. Each is orthogonal to $\Psi$ by step 1.2. Thus $\langle(\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_j)\Psi,\Psi\rangle=-\delta_{ij}$ for all $i,j\in\{x,y,z\}$.

[Directional correlation] By the linearity of [F4], $(\sigma_{a}\otimes\sigma_{b})\Psi=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}(\sigma_{i}\otimes\sigma_{j})\Psi$, so the final identity of step 2.2 and the conjugate-linearity of the inner product in its second argument give $\langle(\sigma_{a}\otimes\sigma_{b})\Psi,\Psi\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{i}b_{j}(-\delta_{ij})=-a\cdot b$, with real $a,b$.

[Joint numbers] Let $a,b$ be unit vectors and $\varepsilon,\delta\in\Sigma$. By step 1.1, $P_{a,\varepsilon}=\tfrac12(I+\varepsilon\sigma_{a})$ and $P_{b,\delta}=\tfrac12(I+\delta\sigma_{b})$, so multilinearity of the tensor product [F4] and the bilinearity of the inner product give $\bigl\langle(P_{a,\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b,\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\langle\Psi,\Psi\rangle+\varepsilon\langle(\sigma_{a}\otimes I)\Psi,\Psi\rangle+\delta\langle(I\otimes\sigma_{b})\Psi,\Psi\rangle+\varepsilon\delta\langle(\sigma_{a}\otimes\sigma_{b})\Psi,\Psi\rangle\bigr)=\tfrac14(1-\varepsilon\delta\,a\cdot b)$ by steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1; this is (c).

[Marginals and correlation] Summing the formula of step 4.1 over the distant label and using $\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\delta=0$ gives $\sum_{\delta}\bigl\langle(P_{a,\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b,\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle=\tfrac14(2-\varepsilon a\cdot b\cdot0)=\tfrac12$, and symmetrically for the other marginal; the correlation is $\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}\varepsilon\delta\,\tfrac14(1-\varepsilon\delta a\cdot b)=\tfrac14\bigl((\sum_{\varepsilon}\varepsilon)(\sum_{\delta}\delta)-a\cdot b\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\varepsilon\delta)^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac14(0-4\,a\cdot b)=-a\cdot b$; this is (d).

[Assembly] Step 1.1 is (a), step 1.2 is (b), step 4.1 is (c) and step 5.1 is (d); only the finite-dimensional tensor calculus of [F1]-[F4] and real arithmetic were used, and no physical interpretation is asserted.

Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the observable and probability
postulate P2, the ideal conditional-measurement postulate P3, the kinematics
and massive-particle model postulate P5 as inherited through the cited
spin-$s$ model and spin-spectrum result (only their internal-factor content
is used here), the
internal-factor assignment of the identical-particle and spin postulate P6 and
the preparation and apparatus discipline P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-ideal-conditional-measurement]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]), together with the
composite, observable and measurement readings of
[[def-nrqm-composites-framework-composite-systems-and-local-readouts]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] and
[[def-nrqm-measurement-framework-declared-measurements-and-instruments]], the
angular momentum readings of
[[def-nrqm-angular-momentum-framework-angular-momentum-observables]] and the
units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice, the hypotheses of the cited
mathematical suppliers. The following vocabulary is used by this page.

**(a) Declared spin-half factors.** A **declared spin-half factor** is the
internal factor $V=\mathbb C^{2}$ of the spin-$s$ model
[[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] with spin label
$s=\tfrac12$, with its orthonormal basis $(e_{+},e_{-})$, the self-adjoint
matrices $J_{i}=\tfrac12\sigma_{i}$ of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clause (e) and the spin
observables $S_{i}:=\hbar J_{i}$, explicitly assigned under P2 on $V$ as sharp observables with unit
$\mathrm{J\,s}$, using the internal-factor assignment of P6 clause (ii). For a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^{3}$ put
$S_{n}:=\sum_{i}n_{i}S_{i}$. Put $A_n:=n\cdot\sigma$. The Pauli identities of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clause (e) give
$A_n^*=A_n$ and $A_n^2=I$ for unit $n$. Each Pauli matrix has trace zero,
so $A_n$ has trace zero; its eigenvalues are $+1,-1$, each once. Thus
$S_n=(\hbar/2)A_n$ has eigenvalues $\pm\hbar/2$ with projections
$$P_{n,\varepsilon}:=\tfrac12\bigl(I+\varepsilon\,n\cdot\sigma\bigr), \qquad \varepsilon\in\Sigma=\{-1,+1\},$$
and the label $\varepsilon$ attached to the projection $P_{n,\varepsilon}$ is
the **sign label** of the outcome; the outcome coordinate is
$\varepsilon\hbar/2$, read in the unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$, while the sign label
itself is dimensionless.

**(b) Declared arrangement.** A **declared spin correlation arrangement**
consists of: the declared composite $V\widehat\otimes V$ of two declared
spin-half factors, with inclusion $\kappa$, in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-nrqm-composites-framework-composite-systems-and-local-readouts]] (a
declared pair of distinguishable subsystems whose assigned spaces are the two
internal factors); a **declared preparation** $\rho\in D(V\widehat\otimes V)$,
the set of density operators on the composite
([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]); and two unit
**setting directions** $a_{0},a_{1}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for the first station and
$b_{0},b_{1}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for the second station. The setting labels are
$I=J=\{0,1\}$.

**(c) Declared local sign measurements.** For the first station and setting
$i\in I$, the **declared local sign measurement** is the declared ideal sharp
measurement whose outcome structure is the pair
$(P_{a_{i},+}\otimes I,\;P_{a_{i},-}\otimes I)$ with the sign labels $\pm1$:
these are the spectral projections of the local readout of the assigned
observable $(S_{a_{i}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ on the declared composite, the local
readout being constructed through the spectral measure by clause (c) of
[[def-nrqm-composites-framework-composite-systems-and-local-readouts]] and
[[lem-nrqm-composites-local-pvm-tensor-extension]]. The second station's
declared local sign measurement for setting $j$ is
$(I\otimes P_{b_{j},+},\;I\otimes P_{b_{j},-})$, defined symmetrically.

**(d) Declared joint sign measurement and tables.** For $(i,j)\in I\times J$
the **declared joint sign measurement** of the setting pair is the declared
ideal sharp measurement of the composite whose outcome structure is
$$E_{ij}:=\bigl(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta}\bigr)_{(\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma}, \qquad E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta},$$
with the pair of sign labels as its labels: by the identities $P_{n,\varepsilon}^*=P_{n,\varepsilon}$,
$P_{n,\varepsilon}^2=P_{n,\varepsilon}$,
$P_{n,+}P_{n,-}=0$ and $P_{n,+}+P_{n,-}=I$ from (a), each factor is an
orthogonal projection, and the tensor calculus of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] gives
$E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)E_{ij}(\varepsilon',\delta')=
\delta_{\varepsilon\varepsilon'}\delta_{\delta\delta'}E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)$
and $\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=I$, so this is a
finite family of mutually orthogonal projections resolving the identity, as
required by clause (a) of
[[def-nrqm-measurement-framework-declared-measurements-and-instruments]]. Its
**outcome law** in the declared preparation $\rho$ is
$$\nu^{\rho}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)\bigr), \qquad (\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma,$$
read from clause (b) of
[[def-nrqm-measurement-framework-declared-measurements-and-instruments]]
(compare P2 clause (ii), [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]).
The **correlation table of the arrangement** is the family
$\nu^{\rho}=(\nu^{\rho}_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$, which is a binary
correlation model on $(I,J)$ in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-bell-binary-correlation-models]] clause (a); its correlations
$E_{ij}(\nu^{\rho})$, its marginals and its CHSH functional $S(\nu^{\rho})$ are
the ones of clauses (b) and (d) of that definition, and are written
$S(\rho;a_{0},a_{1};b_{0},b_{1})$ when the arrangement data are displayed.

**(e) Declared local-response models of the arrangement.** A **declared
local-response model of the arrangement** is a local-response representation,
in the sense of [[def-nrqm-bell-local-response-representation]], of the
correlation table $\nu^{\rho}$. It is a model of the same four tables: it
consists of a probability space of **specifications** and of per-station
response laws, subject to the representation identity, and it need not be a
model of the framework's state space. The arrangement **admits a
local-response model** when such a representation exists.

**(f) Scope.** Clauses (a)-(e) fix model vocabulary. They assign no spatial
position, worldline, spatial separation or temporal order to the two factors;
they assert no dynamics, no interaction, no apparatus, no detection procedure
and no measured correlation; they do not assert that the composite is prepared
by any particular laboratory procedure. Whether a laboratory arrangement
realizes the declared preparation, the declared directions and the declared
sign measurements is a tested identification with uncertainty under P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]), not a consequence of this
definition; the model's assignments of states to preparations and of spectral
projections to quantities are the readings of P1, P2 and P3 fixed on the
earlier pages.

This item fixes finite combinatorial vocabulary for outcome laws of a
two-station comparison. No physical interpretation, measurement model,
dynamics or locality assertion is made here; the physical readings are fixed
on the page of this pair. No choice principle is used.

**(a) Binary correlation model.** Let $I$ and $J$ be finite nonempty sets, the
**setting labels** of the two stations, and put
$\Sigma:=\{-1,+1\}$ for the common **outcome labels**. A **binary correlation
model** on $(I,J)$ is a family
$$\mu=(\mu_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J},\qquad \mu_{ij}:\Sigma\times\Sigma\to[0,1],$$
of functions with the normalization
$$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=1 \qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\in I\times J$$
([[def-finite-sum]]). Each $\mu_{ij}$ is the **joint law** of the setting pair
$(i,j)$: it is the outcome-weight function of a finite probability space on
the four outcomes $\Sigma\times\Sigma$ in the sense of
[[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], and sums over $\Sigma\times\Sigma$
are finite sums.

**(b) Marginals.** For $(i,j)\in I\times J$ the **marginal law of the first
station** and the **marginal law of the second station** are
$$\mu^{A}_{ij}(\varepsilon):=\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta), \qquad \mu^{B}_{ij}(\delta):=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta), \qquad \varepsilon,\delta\in\Sigma .$$

**(c) No-signalling.** The model $\mu$ is **no-signalling** when the marginal
law of the first station does not depend on the distant setting,
$\mu^{A}_{ij}=\mu^{A}_{ij'}$ for all $i\in I$ and all $j,j'\in J$, and the
marginal law of the second station does not depend on the distant setting,
$\mu^{B}_{ij}=\mu^{B}_{i'j}$ for all $j\in J$ and all $i,i'\in I$. The word is
used as a name for this pair of identities about the tables; no spatial or
causal claim is attached to it.

**(d) Correlations and the CHSH functional.** Assume $I=J=\{0,1\}$. The
**correlation** of the setting pair $(i,j)$ and the **CHSH functional** of the
model are the real numbers
$$E_{ij}(\mu):=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma} \varepsilon\,\delta\,\mu_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta), \qquad S(\mu):=E_{00}(\mu)+E_{01}(\mu)+E_{10}(\mu)-E_{11}(\mu).$$

**(e) Status.** Clauses (a)-(d) introduce finite tables, their marginals, the
no-signalling identities and one linear functional of four correlations. They
assert no physical assumption, no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law
for a real apparatus and no statement about nature; the identification of a
laboratory arrangement with a model $\mu$ is a separate physical matter.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis
of the tensor construction cited below. Let $V=\mathbb C^{2}$ carry the
orthonormal basis $(e_{+},e_{-})$ and let
$$\sigma_{x}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_{y}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_{z}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$
be the Pauli matrices of clause (e) of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] in the ordered basis
$(e_{+},e_{-})$; for $a=(a_{x},a_{y},a_{z})\in\mathbb R^{3}$ put
$\sigma_{a}:=a_{x}\sigma_{x}+a_{y}\sigma_{y}+a_{z}\sigma_{z}$, and for
$\varepsilon\in\Sigma=\{-1,+1\}$ put
$$P_{a,\varepsilon}:=\tfrac12\bigl(I+\varepsilon\,\sigma_{a}\bigr).$$
Let $V\widehat\otimes V$ be the completed tensor product with inclusion
$\kappa$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] and let
$$\Psi:=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})-\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\Bigr)\in V\widehat\otimes V, \qquad q:=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})+\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\Bigr).$$
Then:

(a) for every unit $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $\varepsilon\in\Sigma$ the
operator $P_{a,\varepsilon}$ is an orthogonal projection on $V$,
$P_{a,+}+P_{a,-}=I$ and
$P_{a,\varepsilon}P_{a,\varepsilon'}=\delta_{\varepsilon\varepsilon'}P_{a,\varepsilon}$;

(b) $\|\Psi\|=1$ and the four vectors $\Psi,q,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+}),
\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})$ are mutually orthogonal, so
$(\Psi,q,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+}),\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-}))$ is an
orthonormal basis of $V\widehat\otimes V$;

(c) for all unit $a,b\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and all
$\varepsilon,\delta\in\Sigma$,
$$\bigl\langle(P_{a,\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b,\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle =\tfrac14\bigl(1-\varepsilon\delta\,a\cdot b\bigr);$$

(d) the marginals of the four numbers in (c) are
$$\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\bigl\langle(P_{a,\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b,\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle=\tfrac12 =\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\bigl\langle(P_{a,\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b,\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle,$$
and their correlation is
$$\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Sigma}\sum_{\delta\in\Sigma}\varepsilon\,\delta\, \bigl\langle(P_{a,\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b,\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle =-a\cdot b .$$

The lemma is a finite-dimensional computation in the tensor product; it
asserts no preparation, measurement or physical interpretation. The Axiom of
Countable Choice enters only through the construction of the completed tensor
product cited from [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis
of the tensor construction cited below. Let $V=\mathbb C^{2}$ carry the
orthonormal basis $(e_{+},e_{-})$ and let
$$\sigma_{x}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_{y}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_{z}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

$(e_{+},e_{-})$; for $a=(a_{x},a_{y},a_{z})\in\mathbb R^{3}$ put

$\varepsilon\in\Sigma=\{-1,+1\}$ put
$$P_{a,\varepsilon}:=\tfrac12\bigl(I+\varepsilon\,\sigma_{a}\bigr).$$
Let $V\widehat\otimes V$ be the completed tensor product with inclusion
$\kappa$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] and let
$$\Psi:=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})-\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\Bigr)\in V\widehat\otimes V, \qquad q:=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})+\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\Bigr).$$
Then:

(a) for every unit $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $\varepsilon\in\Sigma$ the
operator $P_{a,\varepsilon}$ is an orthogonal projection on $V$,
$P_{a,+}+P_{a,-}=I$ and
$P_{a,\varepsilon}P_{a,\varepsilon'}=\delta_{\varepsilon\varepsilon'}P_{a,\varepsilon}$;

(b) $\|\Psi\|=1$ and the four vectors $\Psi,q,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+}),
\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-})$ are mutually orthogonal, so
$(\Psi,q,\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{+}),\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{-}))$ is an
orthonormal basis of $V\widehat\otimes V$;

observables $S_{i}:=\hbar J_{i}$, explicitly assigned under P2 on $V$ as sharp observables with unit

itself is dimensionless.

spin-half factors, with inclusion $\kappa$, in the sense of clause (a) of

declared pair of distinguishable subsystems whose assigned spaces are the two
internal factors); a **declared preparation** $\rho\in D(V\widehat\otimes V)$,

([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]); and two unit

$b_{0},b_{1}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for the second station. The setting labels are

measurement whose outcome structure is the pair

these are the spectral projections of the local readout of the assigned
observable $(S_{a_{i}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ on the declared composite, the local
readout being constructed through the spectral measure by clause (c) of

[[lem-nrqm-composites-local-pvm-tensor-extension]]. The second station's
declared local sign measurement for setting $j$ is

ideal sharp measurement of the composite whose outcome structure is
$$E_{ij}:=\bigl(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta}\bigr)_{(\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma}, \qquad E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta},$$

orthogonal projection, and the tensor calculus of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] gives
$E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)E_{ij}(\varepsilon',\delta')=

and $\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=I$, so this is a
finite family of mutually orthogonal projections resolving the identity, as
required by clause (a) of

**outcome law** in the declared preparation $\rho$ is
$$\nu^{\rho}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)\bigr), \qquad (\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma,$$

$\nu^{\rho}=(\nu^{\rho}_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$, which is a binary
correlation model on $(I,J)$ in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-bell-binary-correlation-models]] clause (a); its correlations

the ones of clauses (b) and (d) of that definition, and are written
$S(\rho;a_{0},a_{1};b_{0},b_{1})$ when the arrangement data are displayed.

local-response model of the arrangement** is a local-response representation,
in the sense of [[def-nrqm-bell-local-response-representation]], of the
correlation table $\nu^{\rho}$. It is a model of the same four tables: it
consists of a probability space of **specifications** and of per-station
response laws, subject to the representation identity, and it need not be a
model of the framework's state space. The arrangement **admits a
local-response model** when such a representation exists.

position, worldline, spatial separation or temporal order to the two factors;
they assert no dynamics, no interaction, no apparatus, no detection procedure

realizes the declared preparation, the declared directions and the declared
sign measurements is a tested identification with uncertainty under P7

definition; the model's assignments of states to preparations and of spectral
projections to quantities are the readings of P1, P2 and P3 fixed on the
earlier pages.

two-station comparison. No physical interpretation, measurement model,
dynamics or locality assertion is made here; the physical readings are fixed

**setting labels** of the two stations, and put
$\Sigma:=\{-1,+1\}$ for the common **outcome labels**. A **binary correlation

$(i,j)$: it is the outcome-weight function of a finite probability space on
the four outcomes $\Sigma\times\Sigma$ in the sense of
[[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], and sums over $\Sigma\times\Sigma$

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let

$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that

$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently

The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

observable $(S_{a_{i}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ on the declared composite, the local
readout being constructed through the spectral measure by clause (c) of
[[def-nrqm-composites-framework-composite-systems-and-local-readouts]] and
[[lem-nrqm-composites-local-pvm-tensor-extension]]. The second station's
declared local sign measurement for setting $j$ is
$(I\otimes P_{b_{j},+},\;I\otimes P_{b_{j},-})$, defined symmetrically.

**(d) Declared joint sign measurement and tables.** For $(i,j)\in I\times J$
the **declared joint sign measurement** of the setting pair is the declared
ideal sharp measurement of the composite whose outcome structure is
$$E_{ij}:=\bigl(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta}\bigr)_{(\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma}, \qquad E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta},$$
with the pair of sign labels as its labels: by the identities $P_{n,\varepsilon}^*=P_{n,\varepsilon}$,
$P_{n,\varepsilon}^2=P_{n,\varepsilon}$,
$P_{n,+}P_{n,-}=0$ and $P_{n,+}+P_{n,-}=I$ from (a), each factor is an
orthogonal projection, and the tensor calculus of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] gives
$E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)E_{ij}(\varepsilon',\delta')=
\delta_{\varepsilon\varepsilon'}\delta_{\delta\delta'}E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)$
and $\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)=I$, so this is a
finite family of mutually orthogonal projections resolving the identity, as
required by clause (a) of
[[def-nrqm-measurement-framework-declared-measurements-and-instruments]]. Its
**outcome law** in the declared preparation $\rho$ is
$$\nu^{\rho}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta)\bigr), \qquad (\varepsilon,\delta)\in\Sigma\times\Sigma,$$
read from clause (b) of
[[def-nrqm-measurement-framework-declared-measurements-and-instruments]]
(compare P2 clause (ii), [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]).
The **correlation table of the arrangement** is the family
$\nu^{\rho}=(\nu^{\rho}_{ij})_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$, which is a binary
correlation model on $(I,J)$ in the sense of
[[def-nrqm-bell-binary-correlation-models]] clause (a); its correlations
$E_{ij}(\nu^{\rho})$, its marginals and its CHSH functional $S(\nu^{\rho})$ are
the ones of clauses (b) and (d) of that definition, and are written
$S(\rho;a_{0},a_{1};b_{0},b_{1})$ when the arrangement data are displayed.

**(e) Declared local-response models of the arrangement.** A **declared
local-response model of the arrangement** is a local-response representation,
in the sense of [[def-nrqm-bell-local-response-representation]], of the
correlation table $\nu^{\rho}$. It is a model of the same four tables: it
consists of a probability space of **specifications** and of per-station
response laws, subject to the representation identity, and it need not be a
model of the framework's state space. The arrangement **admits a
local-response model** when such a representation exists.

**(f) Scope.** Clauses (a)-(e) fix model vocabulary. They assign no spatial
position, worldline, spatial separation or temporal order to the two factors;
they assert no dynamics, no interaction, no apparatus, no detection procedure
and no measured correlation; they do not assert that the composite is prepared
by any particular laboratory procedure. Whether a laboratory arrangement
realizes the declared preparation, the declared directions and the declared
sign measurements is a tested identification with uncertainty under P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]), not a consequence of this
definition; the model's assignments of states to preparations and of spectral
projections to quantities are the readings of P1, P2 and P3 fixed on the
earlier pages.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $A_0,A_1\in\mathcal B(H)$, $B_0,B_1\in\mathcal B(K)$ be bounded self-adjoint
operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with
$A_i^2=I_H$ and $B_j^2=I_K$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]). Let $H\widehat\otimes K$ be the completed tensor
product of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] and put

$$C:=A_0\otimes(B_0+B_1)+A_1\otimes(B_0-B_1)\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes K).$$

Then:

(a) $C$ is self-adjoint and
$$C^2=4\,I_{H\widehat\otimes K}-[A_0,A_1]\otimes[B_0,B_1];$$

(b) $\|C^2\|\le8$ and $\|C\|\le2\sqrt2$ in the operator norm
([[def-operator-norm]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]);

(c) for all $\psi,\psi'\in H\widehat\otimes K$, $|\langle C\psi,\psi'\rangle|\le2\sqrt2\,\|\psi\|\,\|\psi'\|$
(this is the Tsirelson bound for the stated pair of binary sharp models); consequently the absolute value of the
CHSH combination of the four expectations $\langle(A_i\otimes B_j)\psi,\psi\rangle$ of a unit vector $\psi$ is at
most $2\sqrt2$;

(d) the bound is attained on $H=K=\mathbb C^2$: let $\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ be the Pauli matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]], let
$\Psi:=\frac1{\sqrt2}(e_+\otimes e_--e_-\otimes e_+)$ with the orthonormal basis $(e_+,e_-)$ of $\mathbb C^2$, put
$\sigma_a:=a_x\sigma_x+a_y\sigma_y+a_z\sigma_z$ for a unit vector $a\in\mathbb R^3$, and take
$A_0:=\sigma_z$, $A_1:=\sigma_x$, $B_0:=\sigma_{(z+x)/\sqrt2}$, $B_1:=\sigma_{(z-x)/\sqrt2}$; then
$\langle\sigma_a\otimes\sigma_b\Psi,\Psi\rangle=-a\cdot b$ for all unit $a,b$, and
$\langle C\Psi,\Psi\rangle=-2\sqrt2$, so $|\langle C\Psi,\Psi\rangle|=2\sqrt2$;

(e) a comparison with the stated local model: if in addition $A_0,A_1,B_0,B_1$ are four $\pm1$-valued random
variables on one probability space, then the absolute value of their CHSH combination is at most $2$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-chsh-and-finite-sampling-law]] (a)); this is a statement about that explicitly specified
common-outcome model, not about all theories, and it is not compared here with any reported experiment.

The theorem is a mathematical statement about bounded operators; no measurement, preparation or empirical claim
is asserted.

Adopt the declared spin correlation arrangement of
[[def-nrqm-bell-declared-spin-arrangement]]: the composite
$V\widehat\otimes V$ of two declared spin-half factors with orthonormal basis
$(e_{+},e_{-})$, a declared preparation $\rho\in D(V\widehat\otimes V)$, the
setting directions $a_{0},a_{1},b_{0},b_{1}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and the four
declared joint sign measurements with outcome laws
$$\nu^{\rho}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta) =\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta})\bigr), \qquad P_{a,\varepsilon}=\tfrac12(I+\varepsilon\,a\cdot\sigma) .$$
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice, the hypotheses of
the cited suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), and
take the **singlet preparation**
$$\Psi:=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\kappa(e_{+}\otimes e_{-})-\kappa(e_{-}\otimes e_{+})\Bigr), \qquad \rho_{\Psi}:=T_{\Psi,\Psi},$$
where $T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ is the rank-one operator of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Then:

(a) for every $(i,j)\in\{0,1\}^{2}$ and all $\varepsilon,\delta\in\Sigma$,
$$\nu^{\rho_{\Psi}}_{ij}(\varepsilon,\delta) =\bigl\langle(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta})\Psi,\Psi\bigr\rangle =\tfrac14\bigl(1-\varepsilon\delta\,a_{i}\cdot b_{j}\bigr);$$

(b) the correlations of the arrangement are
$E_{ij}(\nu^{\rho_{\Psi}})=-a_{i}\cdot b_{j}$ and
$$S(\nu^{\rho_{\Psi}}) =-\bigl[a_{0}\cdot b_{0}+a_{0}\cdot b_{1}+a_{1}\cdot b_{0}-a_{1}\cdot b_{1}\bigr] =-\,(a_{0}\cdot(b_{0}+b_{1})+a_{1}\cdot(b_{0}-b_{1}));$$
in particular, for the unit directions
$a_{0}=(0,0,1)$, $a_{1}=(1,0,0)$, $b_{0}=(1,0,1)/\sqrt2$ and
$b_{1}=(-1,0,1)/\sqrt2$ one has $S(\nu^{\rho_{\Psi}})=-2\sqrt2$, so
$\bigl|S(\nu^{\rho_{\Psi}})\bigr|=2\sqrt2>2$;

(c) consequently the correlation table $\nu^{\rho_{\Psi}}$ of the arrangement
at those directions admits no local-response model in the sense of clause (e)
of [[def-nrqm-bell-declared-spin-arrangement]]: there is no local-response
representation of the four tables
([[def-nrqm-bell-local-response-representation]]) with these laws;

(d) the marginal sign laws of the arrangement are
$\nu^{\rho_{\Psi},A}_{ij}(\varepsilon)=\tfrac12=
\nu^{\rho_{\Psi},B}_{ij}(\delta)$ for every setting pair and every direction, so
the table is no-signalling in the sense of clause (c) of
[[def-nrqm-bell-binary-correlation-models]]; and a discarded declared local
instrument on either factor leaves the reduced preparation of the other factor
and every local outcome law of that factor unchanged
([[pthm-nrqm-composites-local-instruments-and-no-signalling]] clause (b)).

The item is a conditional model computation: it asserts no measured
correlation, no apparatus and no empirical fact, and its exclusion is exactly
of the declared local-response class of these four tables. Higher singleton
claims about hidden variables in general are not asserted.

derivations.claim: [CHSH functional as an operator trace] Put $C:=\sigma_{a_{0}}\otimes(\sigma_{b_{0}}+\sigma_{b_{1}})+\sigma_{a_{1}}\otimes(\sigma_{b_{0}}-\sigma_{b_{1}})$, a bounded operator on $V\widehat\otimes V$ by [F3]. For each $(i,j)$, [F2] gives $\sigma_{a_{i}}\otimes\sigma_{b_{j}}=(P_{a_{i},+}-P_{a_{i},-})\otimes(P_{b_{j},+}-P_{b_{j},-})=\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}\varepsilon\delta\,P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta}$, a finite sum, so by [F1], the linearity of the finite sum and the linearity of the trace [F5], $E_{ij}(\nu^{\rho})=\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}\varepsilon\delta\operatorname{tr}(\rho(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta}))=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\sum_{\varepsilon,\delta}\varepsilon\delta(P_{a_{i},\varepsilon}\otimes P_{b_{j},\delta})\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\sigma_{a_{i}}\otimes\sigma_{b_{j}}))$. Summing the four terms with the CHSH signs and using [F3] and the linearity of the trace gives $S(\nu^{\rho})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho\,C)$.
[Operator norm bound] By [F2] the matrices $\sigma_{a_{i}},\sigma_{b_{j}}$ are self-adjoint involutions, so [F6] applies and gives $\|C\|\le2\sqrt2$.

[Trace bound] By [F4] $\rho$ is trace class with $\|\rho\|_{1}=1$, so [F5] makes $\rho C$ trace class with $\|\rho C\|_{1}\le\|\rho\|_{1}\|C\|=\|C\|$, and the trace bound of [F5] gives $|\operatorname{tr}(\rho C)|\le\|\rho C\|_{1}\le\|C\|\le2\sqrt2$. With step 1.1 this is $\bigl|S(\nu^{\rho})\bigr|\le2\sqrt2$, which is (a).

[Attainment; the Axiom of Choice enters through F7 here] Clause (b) is exactly [F7] for the singlet preparation and the displayed directions, and step 2.1 shows that no value larger than $2\sqrt2$ occurs. The Axiom of Choice is required at this proof step to invoke the attainment result with its stated hypotheses; the operator-norm derivation of (a) uses the Countable Choice hypothesis of its mathematical suppliers.

The degenerate involutions A_i=I_H, B_j=I_K are allowed by [F6] and step 1.2; the bound |S|<=2sqrt2 holds there.
